bull.argument: Walmart's core business is growing with its digital channel. U.S. comparable sales rose 4.3% in fiscal 2026, and eCommerce contributed about 4.3 points of that growth, showing that the omnichannel strategy is producing results. Operating income grew to $29,825 million from $29,348 million on net sales growth of 4.7%, and ROA improved to 8.2% from 7.9%. The risks are real. Operating margin slipped 13 basis points, and ROI fell to 15.1% from 15.5% as capital spending rose. The filing also warns that AI-driven shopping could pull traffic from stores. Still, the company is spending on automation and technology from a position of scale, and the reported growth in comparable sales and operating income suggests those investments are earning their keep. The bull case rests on execution continuing to convert that spending into returns.

claims.claim: Walmart U.S. comparable sales grew in fiscal 2026, though at a slightly slower pace than the prior year.
claims.quote: Walmart U.S. comparable sales increased 4.3% and 4.8% in fiscal 2026 and 2025, respectively.

claims.claim: eCommerce is a major driver of U.S. comparable sales growth.
claims.quote: Walmart U.S. eCommerce sales positively contributed approximately 4.3% and 2.9% to comparable sales for fiscal 2026 and 2025

claims.claim: ROI declined in fiscal 2026 because of heavier capital spending, a point the bull case must acknowledge.
claims.quote: The decrease in ROI was primarily due to an increase in average invested capital due to higher purchases of property and equipment.

bear.argument: The bull case leans on growth and returns that the filing itself shows are weakening under heavier spending. Operating margin fell from 4.4% to 4.2%, and ROI declined from 15.5% to 15.1% because average invested capital rose to $310,733 million from $291,444 million, driven by higher purchases of property and equipment. The filing says the cost of eCommerce, technology, talent and automation investments will hurt financial performance in the short term, and that failure to realize their benefits may hurt results over the longer term. Operating income rose only about $477 million on $31.9 billion of extra net sales, so growth in profit is lagging growth in revenue. Comparable sales also depend heavily on digital channels, and the filing warns that shifting traffic online could reduce in-store sales. Management also cites a roughly $0.9 billion rise in self-insured liability claims and a $0.7 billion PhonePe charge. Together, these point to rising costs absorbing the benefit of higher sales.

claims.claim: Return on investment declined as invested capital grew faster than operating returns.
claims.quote: The decrease in ROI was primarily due to an increase in average invested capital due to higher purchases of property and equipment.

claims.claim: The company warns its technology and eCommerce spending will hurt near-term results and may not pay off later.
claims.quote: the cost of certain investments in eCommerce, technology, talent and automation, including any operating losses incurred for those initiatives, will adversely impact our financial performance in the short-term

claims.claim: Operating expenses rose as a share of sales, squeezing margin.
claims.quote: Operating income as a percentage of net sales decreased 13 basis points for fiscal 2026

bull.argument: The opponent is right that margin and ROI slipped, and the bull case should say so. Operating margin fell 13 basis points and ROI fell to 15.1% as invested capital rose. But the filing attributes the margin decline mainly to the self-insured claims, the PhonePe charge and higher depreciation, and it describes strong growth in membership income. Gross profit rate also rose 8 basis points, which shows the core merchandise economics held up. Operating income still grew by about $477 million to $29,825 million. ROA rose to 8.2%, though the filing credits part of that to fair value gains on investments, not operations, so it should not be read as proof of stronger operating returns. The bull case is that the investment cycle is front-loaded. Spending is rising, but the filing shows sales growth, eCommerce contribution and membership income all still expanding. Whether returns recover depends on whether those investments mature, which the filing does not guarantee.

claims.claim: Gross profit rate improved in fiscal 2026, showing core merchandise economics held up despite the margin decline.
claims.quote: increased 8 and 40 basis points for fiscal 2026 and 2025, respectively, when compared to the previous fiscal year

claims.claim: Management attributes the operating margin decline partly to costs but also cites strong membership income growth.
claims.quote: primarily due to the factors described above and strong growth in membership income globally

claims.claim: ROA's rise was driven partly by investment fair value gains, not only operations, so it overstates operating improvement.
claims.quote: The increase in ROA was primarily due to an increase in net income as a result of net increases in the fair value of our equity and other investments

bear.argument: The bull case relies on the claim that the spending cycle is front-loaded, but the filing does not show that payoff. Gross profit rate rose only 8 basis points, while operating margin fell 13 basis points. Much of the margin pressure is not investment-related. Self-insured liability claims rose about $0.9 billion because of industry-wide claim costs, and a $0.7 billion PhonePe charge hit operating expenses. ROA improved partly because of fair value gains on investments, which are not operating returns. ROI fell to 15.1% as invested capital grew to $310,733 million, so each dollar of capital is earning less. Operating income grew about $477 million on roughly $31.9 billion of added sales, a much weaker rate of profit growth. The filing also states that failure to realize the benefits of these investments may adversely impact financial performance over the longer term. The bull case assumes that payoff will come, but the filing treats it as uncertain.

claims.claim: ROA was helped by fair value gains on investments rather than operating improvement.
claims.quote: net increases in the fair value of our equity and other investments

claims.claim: Margin pressure includes costs unrelated to the investment cycle, such as rising claims expense.
claims.quote: The increase for fiscal 2026 was primarily due to higher self-insured general liability claims expense in the U.S. of approximately $0.9 billion

claims.claim: The filing does not guarantee that the investments will pay off.
claims.quote: failure to realize the benefits of these investments may adversely impact our financial performance over the longer term

judge.reasoning: Both sides cite verified quotes, but the bear's evidence is more directly on point: it ties the ROI decline to rising invested capital, quantifies the thin profit growth relative to added sales, and identifies non-investment cost drivers like claims expense. The bull concedes much ground and relies on the unverified-in-substance premise that the investment cycle is front-loaded, which the filing does not guarantee, though the bull does usefully flag membership income and gross profit rate gains.
